author: TFTC21
text:
A bitcoiner lost 1.4 BTC to social engineers who spoofed Google calls for months, broke into his Gmail, watched him contact Trezor, then called pretending to be Trezor. 

They used his own stolen ID and passport photos to manufacture a panic story that got him to type his seed phrase into Chrome.

Your own fear is the scammer's best weapon.

author: TFTC21
text:
New research from @bitcoinpolicy, @cygnal, and Neighborhood Bitcoin surveyed registered voters to find out which Bitcoin messages actually land with everyday Americans. 

The results should change how Bitcoiners talk about Bitcoin.

94% of voters have heard of Bitcoin and 61% want to learn more about owning it. But 74% have little to no trust the dollar will hold its value. The audience is there and the macro tailwind is real.

The messages that work best are the ones that address people's actual concerns about control, safety, security, access, and ease of use. "You decide how much, even if that's just $10" and "You can track the activity yourself" were the top performers. Personal control and low barriers to entry resonate.

The messages that flopped are the ones Bitcoiners love most. "Digital gold" confused focus group participants and ranked near the bottom of all 19 messages tested. Industry jargon doesn't land with normal people.

The most trusted messengers aren't influencers or CEOs. 33% said they'd trust a financial advisor they already work with, 25% a retirement planning expert, and 23% a friend or family member who owns Bitcoin. Everyday Bitcoiners are the most powerful advocates for the next wave of adoption.

After reading the tested messages, "not interested at all" dropped from 39% to 32% and "very or extremely interested" rose from 19% to 24%.

Stop talking about Bitcoin the way Bitcoiners talk about Bitcoin. Start with what people actually care about.
